item.title: Authorization Propagation in Agent2Agent Systems: An Experimental Security Evaluation of Multi-Hop Delegation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delegated Agent2Agent (A2A) workflows create a security problem when the agent sending a request is different from the principal from which the authority originated. This paper evaluates a layered downstream-verification design in a synthetic four-party healthcare reimbursement workflow. The prototype separates current-caller context, transitive authorization evidence, per-hop Ed25519 request authentication, and independent replay state for requests and authorization artifacts. Of 15 adversarial conditions, 14 are rejected; an isolated delegation-path test exposes the absence of semantic authority attenuation. A separate authorized-intermediary experiment shows that a holder of the shared authorization-evidence HMAC key can modify the represented authority and generate valid evidence. In the fixed-depth local benchmark, the full configuration has a median security-processing latency of 5.11 ms and a 3.87 kB serialized payload. The results show the value of separating request authentication from inherited authority while identifying origin-verifiable delegation and semantic attenuation as requirements for stronger A2A authorization propagation.
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Donno, Kashif Mehmood, Katina Kralevska

item.title: More Agents, More Reliable? System-Level Reliability of Multi-Agent LLMs under Operational-Profile Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2611.07140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teams increasingly build software from cooperating large language model (LLM) agents, often assuming more agents mean more reliability. Yet the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule merging the agents' answers. Building on HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, we propose a framework combining it with a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic for multi-agent systems. Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through this network, where the combining rule can itself fail, into a reliability envelope showing which evidence limits it. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest but did not clearly exceed the best, and a voter failing on 5\% of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model. More agents yield a more defensible reliability claim, not automatically a more reliable system.
item.dc:creator: Burkay Tun\c{c}t\"urk, Koorosh Aslansefat, Yiannis Papadopoulos, Bao Nguyen

item.title: Design of Multi-UAV Cooperative Deep Semantic Autoencoders for Communication Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.07374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Driven by the rapid development of the low-altitude economy, Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks have become increasingly important for executing tasks such as search, rescue, and monitoring. However, under bandwidth-constrained scenarios, UAV networks still face significant challenges in task execution efficiency and intelligent processing capabilities. To address these issues, we propose Multi-UAV Cooperative Deep Semantic Autoencoders (MC-DSA) for communication networks. The architecture comprises one Task UAV (T-UAV) and multiple Support UAVs (S-UAVs), which jointly enhance communication efficiency and data-processing capability via semantic communication and cooperation. Specifically, we introduce a semantic matching and source selection mechanism, enabling the proposed MC-DSA to handle low-quality images while ensuring effective utilization of high-quality images. The T-UAV broadcasts a task query, and each S-UAV computes the semantic similarity between its local image and the query. Communication links are established only when the similarity exceeds a predefined threshold. The training algorithm optimizes network parameters through gradient descent, improving semantic feature extraction accuracy. The testing algorithm evaluates UAV collaboration efficiency and communication quality. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with benchmarks, the proposed MC-DSA improves image semantic segmentation accuracy while maintaining task execution efficiency. As a result, it reduces redundant transmissions and offers an effective solution for multi-UAV communication networks.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE Transactions on Vehicular Technology, vol. 75, no. 8, pp. 17063-17077, 2026
item.dc:creator: Xiaoling Han, Bin Lin, Nan Wu, Tony Q. S. Quek

item.title: Designing with Cinematic Language: An Intent-Driven Approach to Human-AI Video Clip Co-Creation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative video models have made video creation more accessible, yet creators still struggle to translate high-level narrative intentions into coherent cinematic expressions. Existing systems primarily rely on prompt refinement or expose isolated camera controls, leaving a gap between what to express and how to film it. We present CineAssist, a human-AI co-creation system that treats cinematic language as an interactive design medium connecting creative intentions with executable video controls. We construct a Cinematic Language Design Space and an annotated dataset from 107 filmmaking sources and 1,436 film clips, linking communicative intentions to cinematic parameter values. CineAssist combines a multi-agent workflow for intent alignment and strategy recommendation with an interactive cinematic editor and a context-sensitive preference learner for user-controlled personalization. We evaluate the system through three studies examining end-to-end usability, cinematic quality, and preference evolution. Results show that CineAssist facilitates efficient, controllable, and personalized intent-driven cinematic video creation.
item.dc:creator: Yi He, Zhengxi Yu, Feilin Han, Chuer Chen, Shengqi Dang, Nan Cao

item.title: Trilemma: How Agents choose between Honesty, Confidentiality, and Task Completion
item.description: arXiv:2611.08312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personal AI agents often act on underspecified instructions and draw on context such as their user's messages and calendar to decide how to proceed. This context can contain private preferences that interfere with the task, with other people's interests, or with confidentiality norms. Prior work has studied deception under goal conflicts and the leakage of private information, but largely as separate problems. We study both problems together in a simulated company Slack workspace in which four employees delegate sprint staffing to personal agents. Two agents learn from private messages that their employee avoids working with a particular colleague. Because the other agents request justifications for task preferences and the only true justification is confidential, the agents cannot simultaneously remain honest, preserve confidentiality, and complete the staffing. We evaluate seven open-weight models and Claude and GPT models. Of the 135/140 open-weight agents that pursue the avoidance preference, 107 either make false claims about task fit or logistics or cite a true consideration as if it were their actual reason. In a three-model comparison, confidentiality instructions reduce disclosure of the preference from 83% (none) to 31% (medium) to 2% (strong). However, the task is often not completed anyway; in the main experiment (medium confidentiality instructions), only 16 of 70 runs end with a valid staffing. In their reasoning traces, agents frequently acknowledge evidence against their claims and still conclude that the claims are not false; they engage in motivated reasoning. Our results indicate that agents can strategically make false or misleading claims in a day-to-day task without being instructed to; the environment provides a controlled testbed for studying how agents resolve such conflicts and for developing deception monitors.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Taraz, Abhinav Kumar, Sahar Abdelnabi

item.title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
item.description: arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.
item.dc:creator: Vivek Acharya

item.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.07066v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.
item.dc:creator: Sungil Son, Hoseong Jung, Dahyun Oh, H. Jin Kim

item.title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.07089v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.
item.dc:creator: Sam Ganzfried

item.title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.07122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.
item.dc:creator: Korbinian K\"ugler, Carolin Schmidt, Florian Dandl, Filipe Rodrigues

item.title: Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover
item.description: arXiv:2611.07307v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects. When taking over a project, they need to recover currently applicable requirements from the interaction history and update them in response to new requests. However, most coding benchmarks do not include long interaction histories, and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. We therefore provide agents with the interaction history, current request, and pre-request project environment, ask them to make the requested changes, and assess takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95%. We then use requirement atoms to independently diagnose a larger set of takeover targets, examining relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction, and current request processing. We further supply correct pre-request or target states to examine the remaining difficulties in requirement processing and project modification. The diagnostics show that none of the six configurations produces fully correct post-request requirement states, and a case illustrates omission of previously recovered constraints during updating. With correct target states supplied, the mean complete-delivery rate is 8.11%, with build and regression pass rates of 96.40% and 90.99%, but target-test success remains 9.01%. These results show difficulties in both forming target requirement states and implementing supplied targets in existing projects. Based on these findings, we introduce ReqMemBench, which combines requirement diagnostics with delivery validation to support systematic evaluation of project takeover.
item.dc:creator: Dingxian Wang, Zhe Fu, Jiaqi Deng, Chao Yin, Ganesh Prabhu, Karthik Gomadam Rajagopal, Darwin Yi, Huan Huo, Guandong Xu, Xianzhi Wang, Andrew Rabinovich, Zhao Chen

item.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2611.07461v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.
item.dc:creator: Haibo Jin, Peng Kuang, Xiaopeng Yuan, Lucheng Fu, Jerry Wang, Xucheng Yu, Yaoning Yu, Dehao Wu, Runguo Li, Colin Su, Jingxuan Sun, Xuyang Liu, Haojing Luo, Haohan Wang

item.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
item.description: arXiv:2611.07483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.
item.dc:creator: Xiaobo Chen, Genliang Zhu, Ziyuan Wang, Chu Wang

item.title: A Bilevel Neurodynamic Approach for Distributed SCAD-Regularized Sparse Least Squares
item.description: arXiv:2611.07618v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.
item.dc:creator: Juntao Li, Qihang Guo, Deyuan Meng

item.title: ReferClaw: Disambiguating User Intent for Egocentric Assistance
item.description: arXiv:2611.07683v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Users of egocentric AI assistants often ask short, ambiguous questions whose intended referents cannot be uniquely resolved from video and dialogue history. For example, "Where did I leave it?" may refer to several previously handled objects. Existing VideoQA systems typically commit to a single interpretation, risking plausible but intention-misaligned answers. We introduce ReferClaw, an agentic framework that formulates egocentric streaming QA as an interactive process: the assistant asks clarifying questions to resolve user intent before answering. Three cooperating agents identify candidate interpretations, request clarification, and generate answers grounded in the resolved intent and visual evidence. A bounded, cost-aware policy balances expected information gain against user effort while limiting clarification turns and question complexity. Referclaw learns from interaction through intent-specific skill updates and process-reward-guided policy optimization with agent-level credit assignment. Evaluations on augmented egocentric QA benchmarks demonstrate improved answer accuracy and joint answer-and-grounding performance over existing baselines, alongside zero-shot transfer across datasets. These findings support interactive clarification as a practical approach to resolving online user intent in egocentric streaming assistance.
item.dc:creator: Hangyu Qin, Junbin Xiao, Angela Yao

item.title: SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments
item.description: arXiv:2611.07996v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Jiming Su, Feng Zhu, Yuhao Xiao, Miao Zhang

item.title: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
item.description: arXiv:2611.08361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team's estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e., gauge drift. In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across $1000$ simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from $0.542$m to $0.140$m in a $50\times50$m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Iyer, Andy Ye, Akshay Narayan, Nora Ayanian

item.title: SCALE: Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.08390v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose SCALE, a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, SCALE matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, SCALE employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate SCALE across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that SCALE significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/.
item.dc:creator: Shanghao Shi, Jian Xiao, Ching-Hsiang Chan, Sanjoy Baruah, Sastry Kompella, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, William Yeoh, Ning Zhang

item.title: MIND: AI Co-Scientist for Material Research
item.description: arXiv:2604.13699v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled agentic AI systems for scientific discovery, but most approaches remain limited to textbased reasoning without automated experimental verification. We propose MIND, an LLM-driven framework for automated hypothesis validation in materials research. MIND organizes the scientific discovery process into hypothesis refinement, experimentation, and debate-based validation within a multi-agent pipeline. For experimental verification, the system integrates Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials, particularly SevenNet-Omni, enabling scalable in-silico experiments. We also provide a web-based user interface for automated hypothesis testing. The modular design allows additional experimental modules to be integrated, making the framework adaptable to broader scientific workflows. The code is available at: https://github.com/IMMS-Ewha/MIND, and a demonstration video at: https://youtu.be/lqiFe1OQzN4.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: In: Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases. Applied Data Science Track, Demo Track and Industrial Track, LNCS 16950, pp. 324-328 (2027)
item.dc:creator: Geonhee Ahn, Donghyun Lee, Hayoung Doo, Jonggeol Na, Hyunsoo Cho, Sookyung Kim

item.title: AgentCue: Statistical Summaries for Guiding Decentralized Multi-Agent Self-Organization
item.description: arXiv:2610.16621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) combine multiple agents to solve complex tasks, and recent MAS scale to more than a thousand agents. At this scale, decentralized MAS remove the central orchestrator that assigns sub-tasks, and the agents, which we call workers, self-organize through their own choices of sub-tasks and collaborators on a shared board. As workers keep adding participation and collaboration records, however, the information explodes: workers spend more and more effort on reading the records of other workers, and self-organization loses efficiency. In the statistical view, we represent the execution history of an MAS by two continually updated networks, a collaboration network among workers and a participation network between workers and task types. We then propose AgentCue, a method built on a new latent space model that places workers and task types in a shared latent space. At each checkpoint, that is, after a fixed number of sessions of the workers, the estimated parameters of the latent space model form a compact and interpretable statistical summary, and workers use the statistical summary to choose sub-tasks and collaborators without repeated searches of the shared board. We also provide theoretical results on model identifiability and estimation accuracy for continually updated networks. Experiments on three benchmarks for cross-document reasoning, mathematical theorem proving, and software patch generation show that AgentCue improves the efficiency, accuracy, and interpretability of self-organization.
item.dc:creator: Guojun Zhu, Xinyou Chen, Kejian Zhang, Zhi Zhang, Sanguo Zhang, Doudou Zhou

item.title: EmboTeam: Asymmetric State Grounding for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2601.11063v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Heterogeneous multi-robot collaboration over long horizons requires both global task planning and robust coordination during execution. Existing plan- ners using large language models (LLMs) can generate task decompositions or symbolic plans, but often execute them as rigid action sequences, making them fragile to local state mismatches and synchronization failures. We propose Em- boTeam, a neuro-symbolic framework for asymmetric state grounding. An LLM generates structured state expectations, which are verified and coordinated through symbolic search using Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) and then grounded into a team-level parallel behavior tree. Robot-specific subtrees per- form precondition checking, skill execution, effect validation, local replanning, and blackboard-based synchronization. We further introduce MACE-THOR, con- taining 42 heterogeneous multi-robot tasks across 8 indoor layouts. EmboTeam improves task success rate from 12% to 55% and goal condition recall from 32% to 75% over LaMMA-P, demonstrating the effectiveness of synchronized reactive grounding for collaboration over long horizons.
item.dc:creator: Haishan Zeng, Mengna Wang, Peng Li

item.title: Set-Valued Routing for Language-Model Agent Systems: A WildChat Benchmark and Cost-Aware Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2606.28925v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language-model agent systems must map natural-language requests to one or more specialized agents before planning or tool execution. This decision is often treated as top-1 selection, although compositional requests can require several capabilities and unnecessary dispatch raises cost. We formulate fixed-catalog routing as set-valued language understanding and construct a benchmark of 3,000 WildChat prompts over 12 capability-defined agents. Reproducible schema-guided reference sets are balanced by agent frequency and route cardinality. We compare profile retrieval, multilabel classifiers, a fine-tuned text encoder, and catalog-conditioned zero-shot GPT-4o. Evaluation combines set quality, latency, capability coverage, and ordinal-cost utility. The encoder attains 89.59 F1, compared with 71.79 for linear SVM and 41.51 for GPT-4o, and retains 88.02 F1 under a harder semantic-group split. We further introduce Weighted Agent Routing (WAR), a deterministic post-scoring rule that changes the quality-cost operating point without retraining; Encoder+WAR obtains the best constrained utility. The results show that catalog-specific supervision and explicit set construction are important for multi-agent dispatch, while cost-aware decision layers can complement strong language encoders.
item.dc:creator: Ananto Nayan Bala, Faisal Muhammad Shah

item.title: From Siloed Algorithms to Compliance-First Agentic Platforms: A Multi-Layered Architecture for Hospital AI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2608.06112v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hospitals are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence for triage, imaging, scheduling etc., yet most deployments remain isolated point solutions locked inside departmental silos, resulting in duplicated effort, hidden risks, and unrealized enterprise value. Despite explosive growth of AI in healthcare market and accelerating investment, an estimated 70-80% of healthcare AI pilots fail to scale, largely due to governance gaps, fragmented data, and missing integration blueprints. This research proposes a hospital-specific, compliance-first, Agentic AI architecture with multiple interoperable layers, extending existing hospital AI platform models with: (i) an Agent Orchestration Layer for multi-agent workflows across clinical, operational, and financial domains, (ii) a Compliance and Policy Layer that centralizes policy-as-code for HIPAA, GDPR, the EU AI Act, DISHA Act, India's DPDP Act, and ISO/IEC security and safety standards, and (iii) a Privacy-Preserving Data Fabric that plugs federated learning, differential privacy, and secure enclaves into real-world Hospital Information Management System (HIMS) flows. Using a synthetic but structurally realistic hospital dataset and an open, ready-to-deploy prototype implementation, this study demonstrates the end-to-end orchestration of triage risk prediction, workflow optimization, and compliance logging, achieving substantial simulated reductions in task turnaround times and manual documentation effort while maintaining policy-guarded data access. The resulting architecture offers hospital leaders a pragmatic blueprint to move from ad hoc tools to a governed, globally compliant, ROI-focused AI platform that can be tailored to on-premise, hybrid and cloud-native deployments.
item.dc:creator: Manideep Dhar, Ritwik Singh, Sharat Chandra Kumar Manikonda

item.title: Networked Admissibility-Preserving Control for Directed Safe Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2609.09384v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper addresses safe coordination of scalar agents with constrained input dynamics over fixed rooted digraphs. We propose a networked Admissibility-Preserving Control (APC) architecture for a common moving output corridor under heterogeneous asymmetric input bounds, wherein the Admissibility-Preserving Input Realization (APIR) generates the physical inputs. In logarithmic barrier coordinates, the closed-loop dynamics form an exact cascade of exponentially decaying realization errors and directed consensus dynamics. We derive direction-specific compatibility conditions that guarantee uniform corridor and input margins, bounded commands, unique complete solutions, and exponential consensus for compact initial sets. The closed-form expression for the agreement value quantifies the effect of the initial APIR mismatch. Under the corresponding compatibility conditions, partial pinning guarantees safe reference tracking whenever the root component contains at least one informed agent. Simulations illustrate the coordination guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Abhinav Sinha, Lohitvel Gopikannan, Shashi Ranjan Kumar

item.title: TANGO: RNA Topology and Geometry Co-Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.20277v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Designing RNA sequences that satisfy target tertiary-structure objectives is an important problem in RNA engineering, with broad applications in synthetic biology and therapeutics. Existing 3D RNA design methods have made substantial progress, but they largely treat the target fold as a geometry-only objective. This is incomplete for RNA, whose functional folds are specified not only by tertiary geometry but also by secondary base-pairing topology. We therefore formulate RNA inverse design as a topology-and-geometry co-design problem and propose TANGO, a multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for this task. TANGO adopts a staged curriculum: it first learns a topology-aware policy from secondary-structure targets, then transfers this policy to tertiary-structure targets to train a general co-design model, and finally applies frontier-guided fine-tuning to refine target-specific trade-offs among secondary-structure fidelity, tertiary-structure fidelity, and sequence diversity. Experiments show that TANGO generates diverse and novel designs, improving tertiary- and secondary-structure performance by 18.3% and 52.7%, respectively, over the strongest baseline.
item.dc:creator: Tianmeng Hu, Biao Luo, Ke Li

item.title: Bayesian Replicator Dynamics and the Inversion of Strict Dominance in Bimatrix Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.36345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Replicator dynamics, the central model of evolutionary game theory, describe populations evolving under selection and agents learning by trial and error. They also admit a third use: continuous-time Bayesian inference, in which an agent planning against an opponent accumulates evidence for each candidate strategy. Here we show that this use divides all two-player games into two classes. With the standard expected-utility payoff, the dynamics can be expressed as Bayesian updating only in games (with any number of actions) where no player has a dominant strategy. The logarithmic payoff of Ay and Erb (2005) admits the Bayesian representation in every game. Coordination, anti-coordination, and cyclic games share qualitative dynamics under both payoff definitions, with equilibria displaced and selection thresholds shifted. In contrast, the flows of every game with a dominant strategy are reversed between the payoff definitions, with the strictly dominant strategy eliminated under logarithmic payoffs. Cooperation therefore emerges in the Prisoner's Dilemma, and games of common interest converge to mutual defection. For two-action games the classification is complete and rests on an exact Hamiltonian structure shared by both payoff definitions. The structure gives a behavioural test: cycles in the classic Matching Pennies game have amplitude-independent period (isochronous) under logarithmic payoffs, but not under expected utility. Logarithmic evidence integration thus determines which strategic outcomes dynamical selection can reach, wherever learning approximates Bayesian updating.
item.dc:creator: Jaime Ruiz-Serra, Nihat Ay, Michael Harr\'e
